skyline.text: Seven billion people, a million podcasts, and only one of you
Ajay Shah would rather play cricket than watch Tendulkar
When two opposite interview styles collided in a remote recording

footnote.text: Anybody can start a podcast without spending anything except their time.

brief.head: Speed it up
brief.text: Our brains can take in 500 words a minute, Amit Varma said. Raise listening speed in steps until one stops feeling normal: that is your level. {049-C02}

brief.head: Cursed by knowing
brief.text: Know a subject too well and you assume listeners share your baseline, Varma warned. In audio they cannot go back, so set scenes and introduce voices quickly. {049-C10}

brief.head: Patience pays
brief.text: Work for love and you keep improving; chase the numbers and you lose your soul. Creators overestimate the short term and underestimate the long, Varma said. {049-C19}

brief.head: Loved by a few
brief.text: Many channels can average about fifteen seconds of viewing; Varma’s listening sessions average about forty minutes. Better to be loved by a few than liked by many, he said. {049-C20}

brief.head: Do it in Hindi
brief.text: English podcasts in India are saturated, Varma said. If your English is a hundred and your Hindi eighty, do Hindi: that audience needs you more. {049-C21}

thought.text: Perfection is the enemy of production.
thought.who: Vinay Sitapati’s advice to Amit Varma, passed on to every hesitant creator

lead.kicker: Amit Varma gives away his podcasting course
lead.head: The long and short of podcasting
body: Amit Varma used to teach a three-week course on podcasting. He has decided never to teach it again. In this episode he gave the whole thing away, promising to talk “as long as the light lasts”.
Ajay Shah introduced him as the man who pioneered the podcast in India, before he “became a world famous inventor and producer of a YouTube show”.

Varma began with a confession. When *The Seen and the Unseen* started seven years ago, he planned episodes of 15 or 20 minutes, sure that attention spans were short. “I was wrong about everything I thought I knew about podcasting,” he said.

The episodes grew to three and four hours, then to oral histories of seven and eight hours. “And as it got longer and longer, I got more and more love from people.” {049-S01} By his conservative estimate, listeners have spent about 20 million hours with the show.
## The case for audio

Audio, Varma said, is not YouTube without the video. People listen while commuting, running or washing dishes, so they are a captive audience. Many listen at higher speeds and lose no nuance. And they want depth, which the rest of the media, a mile wide and an inch deep, does not give them.
“Attention spans are not the problem,” he said. {049-C01}
Nor is a podcast radio on demand. Radio, in his metaphor, speaks to four people in a car. “Podcasting is a voice in your head.” {049-C04}

That intimacy brings two imperatives: respect listeners, who are accomplished people and often know more than the host, and be yourself. Asked which gap in the market to fill, Varma replied: “There is only one gap in the market. You aren’t there.” {049-C05}
## Stories and conversations
Varma divides podcasts into two kinds: storytelling and conversation.

For storytellers, his tips came from writing: one piece of information at a time, show rather than tell, beware the curse of knowledge, and make every sentence and sound effect take the story forward or deeper. One person is enough, he said, as Dan Carlin’s *Hardcore History* proves.
For conversations, the rules are about the guest. Ignore conventions of length. Define your purpose. Do your research. Never interrupt. Follow the flow, not the list of questions.
Shah, asking the questions, added examples of his own: Paul Simon on why songs are linear, and a friend who learnt new things from one episode about a man she had known for fifteen years.
## Get it done

The last lessons were for creators. Have a bias for action. Play the long game, because organic growth is exponential and looks like nothing for a long time. Be loved by a few rather than liked by many. And think out of the box, including about which language to podcast in.
Varma had slides on equipment too, but the light was running out. He squeezed in advice on microphones and promised a document of notes in the show notes.
His verdict on cost: “The spoiler alert is that you can really do it for very cheap or you can do it for free.” {049-C22}
His last words went back to his first lesson for creators: “Have a bias for action, don’t hesitate.”

second.label: Turning down a laureate
second.head: Three hours or nothing
second.deck: Amit Varma said no to a Nobel winner in the week of his prize
body: A publisher rang Amit Varma with an offer: fly to Delhi and record with Abhijit Banerjee in the week he won the Nobel Prize. Varma asked for three hours. The publisher offered one. He said no. {049-S08}

One hour, he said, would have meant talking only about what Banerjee won the prize for, RCTs, a narrow subject. With three, Varma wanted to begin in 1963, when Banerjee’s father taught his own father at Presidency College, Calcutta: “a prehistory of the man”.
Given five to eight hours, he could imagine never mentioning the work at all. People and their journeys interest him more. And there are, he said, “fifty other people who will record with you”.

quote.text: I don’t care what kind of celebrity you are.

second.caption: turning down a Nobel laureate

third.head: Not a word from the host
body: Amit Varma asked Mrinal Pande his first question. She then spoke for more than an hour, and he did not say a word. {049-S12}
In a mix of Hindi and English, she took listeners from her childhood in the 1950s to the end of the 1970s: her parents, her mother, her sisters, her coming of age as a woman.

“And it would have been a disaster to interrupt at any point,” Varma said. A younger, callower version of himself might have done it; other interviewers would have cut in after two minutes, and she would never have gone so deep.
Not interrupting is an article of faith for him. Most of us, he said, quoting Stephen Covey, “listen to respond, we don’t listen to understand.” {049-C14}
third.caption: Mrinal Pande’s first answer

sections.label: Why audio
sections.head: Captive, quick and deep
sections.caption: when, how and why we listen
body: When Amit Varma began *The Seen and the Unseen*, he thought listeners had to be grabbed in 15 seconds and let go within 20 minutes. Three reasons proved him wrong.
The first is when people listen: commuting, working out, doing chores. A runner is a captive audience.

The second is how. “Our brain can comprehend up to five hundred words a minute,” Varma said, while we speak at 160 to 200. {#brain} Raise the speed in steps, to 1.2x and then 1.5x, until one step stops feeling normal: that is your natural level. {049-C02}
## Mush at six times
Varma listens to most things at 2x, and up to 3x for research. Krish Ashok once told him of a blind colleague who listens at 6x. “Now you see the plasticity of the brain,” he said. {049-S02}

The third reason is why. Everybody craves depth, Varma argued, and the rest of the media is a mile wide and an inch deep. “Attention spans are not the problem. When you want to go deep, you can go deep. And the most efficient way of going deep is audio.” {049-C01}

Ajay Shah, for whom faster listening was “a very new discovery”, disagreed on depth. “Most humans want diversion,” he said; only a tiny fraction crave depth, and that is enough. Varma replied that everyone has the capacity for it.
~ His first episode with Karthik Muralidharan ran three hours and fifteen minutes. Transcribed, it came to 45,000 words, half a regular book. {#muralidharan}

quote.text: And one should not be judgmental about what you listen at. What you listen at is what you listen at.

sections.label: Why podcasts
sections.head: Not radio with a pause button
sections.caption: a voice in your head
body: Ajay Shah’s first thought was that podcasting was time-shifted radio: the 9 pm news his father once tuned in for, now on demand. Amit Varma said it is fundamentally different.
In India, he said, licence fees for an FM channel are incredibly high, so stations chase the lowest common denominator to recoup them. {#fm} FM is not even allowed to do news.

A podcast costs nothing but time and needs no licence. So it can find niches nobody suspected, such as listeners for eight-hour conversations: a niche that, Varma said, “did not know it existed”. {049-C03}
## Closer and closer

Cinema is a big screen far away, made for westerns and car chases. Television sits two or three metres off and suits sitcoms; YouTube is half a metre away. Radio speaks to four people in a car. “Podcasting is a voice in your head,” Varma said. {049-C04}
So voice modulation would be a bug, not a feature. One listener of his episode with Abhinandan Sekhri felt so at home that he interrupted the recording. {049-S03}

~ Shah had his own evidence. Anjali Sharma had known Josh Felman for fifteen years, yet his episode told her things that were new. Felman’s reply: “You never asked me, otherwise I would have always told you.” {049-S04}

quote.text: I felt so much that I’m sitting in a living room talking to two of my friends that at one point I interrupted you.
quote.who: A listener, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: Two imperatives
sections.head: Respect them, be yourself
sections.caption: respecting listeners and being yourself
body: Old media had the few talking down to the many, Amit Varma said: condescending, patronising, lecturing. An intimate medium does not allow it.
Listeners are accomplished people who in many ways know more than the host. So the first imperative is to respect their time and speak to them as human beings. No artifice, he said, is required.

The second is to be authentic. When a participant in his podcasting course asked whether there was a gap in the market to fill, Varma said it was a terrible way to think. Among more than seven billion people, only one thing sets you apart: that you are you. {049-C05}
## A journey, not a market

*The Seen and the Unseen*, he said, is his intellectual journey: he calls people he wants to know more about, not people in the news. Listeners on a similar journey, at whatever point, will come along.

Asked by Ajay Shah whether he designs for loyal fans or occasional visitors, Varma said he does not think of the audience at all: “Ekla chalo re”, walk alone, “and then whoever comes comes along”. {049-J15}

~ A loyal audience that turns up every Friday is already forming for *Everything is Everything*, Varma said. Even so, when the two started the show, he asked Shah not to look at the numbers for two years, about 104 episodes. {049-S16}

quote.text: There is only one gap in the market. You aren’t there.

sections.label: Storytelling
sections.head: One thing at a time, please
sections.caption: telling stories for the ear
body: A reader can go back over a sentence. A listener washing dishes cannot, Amit Varma said, so audio should give one piece of information at a time. {049-C06}

His print example had “the famous podcaster Amit Varma”, while conducting a webinar from his home office in Andheri, arrested by the Delhi police for polluting Delhi with his convoluted classes. The audio version opened: “The famous podcaster Amit Varma is behind bars.”
Ajay Shah recalled Paul Simon on poems and songs: the mind goes over a poem many times, but “Songs are linear. So you don’t get a second take.” {049-S06}
## Show, don’t tell

Listeners stay, Varma said, because they care about a character and want to know how a conflict resolves. Kurt Vonnegut’s rule: every character must want something, even if it is only a glass of water. {049-C07}

Showing means fewer adjectives and more verbs, as in the film cliché of the scene where a character pets a dog. “All of the action of the world, all of the interest in the world is in verbs.” {049-C08}

~ Every sentence, and every sound effect, must take the story forward or deeper. *Everything is Everything* learnt this with on-screen inserts: these days, a mention of Karl Marx brings no photo of him. {049-C09}

quote.text: Because what draws us into the story, it is that wanting, it is that desire.

sections.label: Conversation
sections.head: Out of autocomplete mode
sections.caption: the art of conversation
body: Amit Varma does not interview people, he said; he has conversations. His first rule is to ignore conventions of length, and he credits himself with shifting India’s Overton window: two- and three-hour episodes are now normal.

Form dictates content. For a five-minute show you need not read the guest’s book; for half an hour, a ChatGPT summary will do; for an hour, you must read it. For eight hours, read everything they have written, and care about their life. {049-C11}

Authors arrive with prepared sound bites, able to talk on autopilot. Varma asks about childhood and home, and lets himself be vulnerable. “And my task is to take them out of autocomplete mode.” {049-C12}
## Follow the thread
Panel moderators, he said, are often thinking of question seven while the guest answers question six. He prepares themes in depth, in no fixed order. “That path is where the magic lies.” {049-C15}
For his longest episodes he works with “three overlapping scaffoldings”: the guest’s life, their work, and themes and ideas. {049-C16}

~ Clarity includes tense. Ajay Shah recalled being thrown, in the episode on the 1991 reforms, by Shruti Rajagopalan narrating history in the present tense. His rule: past tense for the past. {049-S13}

quote.text: And then I will find that I haven’t used eighty per cent of the prep that I have done, and it doesn’t matter.

sections.label: For creators
sections.head: Doers versus whiners
sections.caption: a bias for action
body: Abraham Lincoln, Amit Varma recalled, would spend five of six hours sharpening the axe before chopping down a tree. {049-J14} That suits policy, Varma said, but creators should do the opposite. “If you’re faced with a choice of getting it right and getting it done, I want you to get it done.” {049-C17}
Everyone is bad at first; he tells people to hear *The Seen and the Unseen* in reverse order. “You have to cut the tree to learn how to cut the tree.”

Ajay Shah’s motto since childhood is that life is not a spectator sport: playing cricket himself matters more than watching Sachin Tendulkar. He wants a culture that treasures people’s best work, so that everyone is readier to start. {049-C18}

At the XKDR Forum anniversary party, asked to complete “There are two kinds of people in the world”, Varma had said: the doers and the whiners. {#whiners} “And you have described the whiners,” he told Shah.
## The long game
The YouTuber Ali Abdaal reached his thousandth subscriber only around his fiftieth video. His later advice: two videos a week for two years, without looking at the numbers. {049-S15}
~ Shah added that an inauthentic show can last only so long before its maker loses interest.

quote.text: Now most people are not going to make fifty videos when they have less than a thousand subscribers.

side.boxText: Amit Varma taught a three-week podcasting course twice a year, to a niche audience. He has now decided he will never teach it again. Instead, he said, he wants to give away everything he has learnt. {#course}

contQuote.text: So the kind of form will dictate the kind of content. And the kind of content will dictate your character. It will change you. You do a longer podcast, you will listen much more.

p3.title: Stories from the studio
p3.deck: A railway driver, an unmentioned book, a clipped guest and a generous one

stories.start: Now there are two iconic uh sort of landmarks in radio history
stories.end: his villagers considered him to be a good guy or even sing about that
stories.caption: the ballad of a railway driver
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a 1957 landmark of radio, and show, don’t tell
stories.head: The driver who stayed on board
body: John Axon was a railway driver. At one point, Amit Varma said, he was driving a train that he knew he could not control: it was going to careen out. {049-S07}
He had two choices. He could jump and save himself, or stay on the train and do whatever he could to save lives up ahead. He stayed on the train, and he died.

A group of people wrote a bunch of songs about him. They also went to his village and recorded interviews with the people who had known him, with no plan to use any of it. They took the sound of the train, the background, the family, someone crying.

“And then they had the master stroke that why don’t we use all of this?” Varma said. “And they used it.” The result was *The Ballad of John Axon*, from 1957, which Varma was unsure whether to call a play or an album. {049-R03}
Hearing somebody who knew Axon talk about him, Varma said, tells you far more than being told that his villagers considered him a good guy.

He paired it with a second landmark, *Sun of the Family*, a Danish radio show from around 1997 about a young musician who killed himself. Its producers spoke to his parents, his brother and his girlfriend. {049-R04}
~ “It is heartbreaking when you listen to it,” Varma said. In the inflection of their voices and in their particular memories, a whole person comes to life.
stories.why: This is show, don’t tell in sound. Hearing the people who knew a man talk about him does more than any narrator’s adjective, and Varma’s rule for all storytelling is fewer adjectives, more verbs. {049-C08}
stories.postscript: Varma did not know whether *Sun of the Family* is online, and asked listeners to put it in the comments if it is.

stories.start: I was once a couple of years back in Bangalore recording some six episodes
stories.end: but you won't get what I spoke to him for five hours about
stories.caption: an all-night preparation
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on preparing hard, then letting it go
stories.head: Notes for a book never mentioned
body: On a trip to Bangalore, recording some six episodes in seven days, Amit Varma was due to record one morning with Sugata Srinivasaraju, who had just published a massive book on Deve Gowda, *Furrows in a Field*. {049-R13}
He stayed up all night and wrote several thousand words of notes on it. “The next day we met, we spoke for five and a half hours, we did not mention the book.” {049-S09}

Srinivasaraju’s life, the milieu he grew up in and how he watched his city transform were so fascinating that the book was never needed. And Varma is his own boss: no radio station was telling him to spend 45 minutes on the book.
~ Search YouTube for Sugata on Deve Gowda, he said, and you find fifty talks and forty panel discussions, but not what they spoke about for five hours.
stories.why: Preparation is not for showing off. Varma says he often finds he has not used 80 per cent of his prep, and it does not matter: it is what lets him follow a better conversation. {049-C13}

stories.start: Tyler Carwin, just a great podcast and an intellectual I admire so much.
stories.end: if I recorded a five hour episode with him I treat it really differently
stories.caption: two opposite styles colliding
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a guest he admires, and a flow that never came
stories.head: Ask, answer, stop, repeat
body: Amit Varma admires Tyler Cowen, whose interviewing style is, in a sense, the polar opposite of his own. {#cowen} Cowen brings a set of great prepared questions, “the kind of questions that someone like me is not even capable of coming up with”, and goes through them one after another.
Then Cowen came on *The Seen and the Unseen*, in a remote recording. Varma asked a question; Cowen answered it and stopped. Another question, another clipped answer. {049-S10}
Varma never found the flow he looks for. “It’s not his fault, it’s not my fault, we are who we are,” he said.
~ If he recorded five hours with Cowen today, he said, he would treat it very differently. There is no right or wrong way to do it.

quote.text: So it’s a weird kind of like two opposite styles colliding.

stories.postscript: Varma once complained that Ajay Shah’s answers were too short as well. Shah, he says, has loosened up a lot since.

stories.start: And someone related this anecdote to me that there was some book event
stories.end: That is okay, but have you heard his episode with Shanta J.
stories.caption: one guest recommending another
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on guests who send listeners to other guests
stories.head: Have you heard the other one?
body: In mid-April, a couple of days before this episode was recorded, Jerry Pinto and Shanta Gokhale were signing books in adjoining queues at a book event. A reader told Pinto that his episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* had been transformational. {049-S11}
Pinto’s reply, as it was related to Amit Varma: “That is okay, but have you heard his episode with Shanta ji?”
Gokhale’s episode ran eight and a half hours. She is 83, and when someone asked why so long, Varma answered: “One hour for each decade of her life. Are you telling me that is sufficient?” {049-J05}
~ Pinto’s own episode ran eight hours. In it, Varma and Pinto teared up together while talking about their mothers. {049-R17}
stories.why: One guest sending a fan to another is validation of a rare kind. It also shows Varma’s method at work: when the host is vulnerable, guests drop their prepared sound bites and open up in return. {049-C12}

quiz.q: Which three things, according to Amit Varma, explain why audio listeners will stay for hours?
quiz.a: When they listen, how they listen and why: captive, at higher speeds, wanting depth.

quiz.q: How fast does Krish Ashok’s blind colleague listen to audio, and what does it show?
quiz.a: At 6x, which shows how far the brain’s plasticity lets it adjust.

quiz.q: In Varma’s distance metaphor, if radio is four people in a car, what is a podcast?
quiz.a: A voice in your head, which he calls the most intimate medium.

quiz.q: Why did Varma turn down an episode with an economist in his Nobel Prize week?
quiz.a: The publisher offered one hour; he wanted three, to start in 1963.

quiz.q: What kept confusing Ajay Shah in the episode on the 1991 reforms with Shruti Rajagopalan?
quiz.a: She narrated past events in the present tense, a modern American habit, he said.

quiz.q: If your English is a hundred and your Hindi eighty, what does Varma advise?
quiz.a: Do Hindi: English podcasts are saturated, and that audience needs you more.
